title: Representing organic molecules and functional groups
html:
Guiding question

How does the classification of organic molecules help us to predict their properties?

Carbon forms millions of compounds because it makes four strong covalent bonds, bonds to itself to form chains and rings, and forms multiple bonds. Organic chemists sort these compounds into families (homologous series) by their functional group. Members of one family react in the same way and show smooth trends in physical properties. So if you can name a compound and spot its functional group, you can predict its behaviour. At HL, spectroscopy (MS, IR and ¹H NMR) is used to work out an unknown structure.

S3.2.1 Representing organic molecules

Take butane: its molecular formula C₄H₁₀ shows the number of each type of atom; its displayed formula shows every atom and bond; its structural formula CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ shows how the atoms are arranged; and its skeletal formula is just a zigzag of three lines, showing the carbon backbone.

Type of formulaWhat it showsExample: butan-1-ol
EmpiricalSimplest whole-number ratio of atomsC₄H₁₀O
MolecularActual number of each atom in a moleculeC₄H₁₀O
Full structural (displayed)Every atom and every bond drawnAll C–H, C–C, C–O and O–H bonds drawn out
Condensed structuralThe atoms bonded to each carbon, with no bonds drawnCH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH
SkeletalCarbon chain as a zigzag; each end/corner is a C; H on C not shown; functional groups shownA zigzag of four carbons ending in –OH
Stereochemical (3-D)Shape: wedges (towards you) and dashes (away from you)Used for chiral centres and tetrahedral carbons

Reading a skeletal formula: each line is a C–C bond and each end or corner is a carbon. Because carbon always makes four bonds, you can work out the hydrogens: an end carbon already making one bond carries three H; a carbon in the middle of a chain making two bonds carries two H.

  • Benzene, C₆H₆, is drawn in skeletal form as a hexagon with a circle inside (the delocalized π system); the C₆H₅– group is called phenyl.
  • Condensed formulas may use brackets for branches or repeats: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH is 2-methylpropan-1-ol; CH₃(CH₂)₄CH₃ is hexane.
  • A condensed formula must be unambiguous. Write CH₃CHO for an aldehyde (not CH₃COH, which looks like an alcohol) and CH₃COOH or CH₃CO₂H for a carboxylic acid.
Exam tipIn a skeletal formula, count carbons carefully: every corner and every line end is a carbon atom carrying enough H atoms to make four bonds. Heteroatoms (O, N, Cl…) and the H atoms bonded to them must be drawn.

A skeletal formula shows a zigzag of four carbons with no other atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does the molecule have?

Two end carbons carry 3 H each (6) and two middle carbons carry 2 H each (4): 10. It is butane, C₄H₁₀.

S3.2.2 Functional groups and classes of compound

A functional group is the atom or group of atoms that gives a compound its characteristic chemical reactions: the reactive part of the molecule. The rest of the molecule (the hydrocarbon part) is often written as R. Compounds with the same functional group belong to the same class.

ClassFunctional group (name)Prefix / suffixExampleGeneral formula
Alkanenone (only C–C and C–H)-aneethane, CH₃CH₃CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
AlkeneC=C (alkenyl)-enepropene, CH₂=CHCH₃CₙH₂ₙ
AlkyneC≡C (alkynyl)-yneethyne, HC≡CHCₙH₂ₙ₋₂
Halogenoalkane–X, X = F, Cl, Br, I (halogeno)fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-chloroethane, CH₃CH₂ClCₙH₂ₙ₊₁X
Alcohol–OH (hydroxyl)-ol (hydroxy-)ethanol, CH₃CH₂OHCₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
EtherR–O–R′ (ether)alkoxy-methoxyethane, CH₃OCH₂CH₃CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O
Aldehyde–CHO (carbonyl at chain end)-alethanal, CH₃CHOCₙH₂ₙO
KetoneR–CO–R′ (carbonyl within the chain)-onepropanone, CH₃COCH₃CₙH₂ₙO
Carboxylic acid–COOH (carboxyl)-oic acidethanoic acid, CH₃COOHCₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH
EsterR–COO–R′ (ester)alkyl …-oatemethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃CₙH₂ₙO₂
Amine–NH₂ (amino)-amine (amino-)ethanamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂CₙH₂ₙ₊₁NH₂
Amide–CONH₂ (amido)-amidepropanamide, CH₃CH₂CONH₂—
Nitrile–C≡N (nitrile)-nitrilepropanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN—
Arene–C₆H₅ (phenyl)phenyl- / -benzenemethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₃—
Common mistakeName amines with the locant: CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ is propan-1-amine, not "propanamine". And the general formula of a carboxylic acid is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH (equivalently CₙH₂ₙO₂ counting all the carbons).

Saturated compounds contain only single C–C bonds (alkanes); unsaturated compounds contain C=C or C≡C bonds (alkenes, alkynes). Aliphatic compounds have no benzene ring; aromatic compounds contain one.

Common mistakeAldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and amides all contain C=O, so the C=O alone does not tell you the class. Look at what else is on the carbonyl carbon: H (aldehyde), two C (ketone), OH (acid), O–C (ester), N (amide). An ether has C–O–C with no C=O.

A molecule contains the group –COO– with a carbon on each side. Which class does it belong to?

  1. Carboxylic acid
  2. Ester
  3. Ether
  4. Ketone

C=O with an O–C on the carbonyl carbon is an ester. A carboxylic acid has O–H instead of O–C; an ether has no C=O.

10-second organic quiz

Your class "10-second quiz" molecules are good practice: limonene (alkene), aspirin (carboxylic acid + ester + benzene ring), vanillin (aldehyde + ether + phenol OH), testosterone (ketone + alcohol + alkene), carbamazepine (amide).

More from the quiz: name the functional groups in methamphetamine, serotonin, thujone and menthol
  • Methamphetamine: secondary amine and a benzene ring.
  • Serotonin (a neurotransmitter linked to mood and appetite): primary amine, a secondary amine N–H in the ring, and an –OH on a benzene ring (a phenol).
  • Thujone (found in wormwood): ketone.
  • Menthol: alcohol.

Vanillin, the flavour of vanilla, contains which set of functional groups?

  1. Ketone, ester, alcohol
  2. Carboxylic acid, ether, alkene
  3. Aldehyde, ether, phenol (–OH on a benzene ring)
  4. Aldehyde, ester, amine

Vanillin has a –CHO group, a –OCH₃ ether group and an –OH on the benzene ring.

title: Homologous series, physical properties and IUPAC naming
html:
S3.2.3–S3.2.4 Homologous series and trends in physical properties

DefinitionA homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and the same general formula, in which successive members differ by a –CH₂– unit. Members have similar chemical properties and show a gradual trend in physical properties.

A general formula is a formula that applies to every member of a series, e.g. CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for alkanes or ROH for alcohols, where n is an integer.

Boiling point increases with chain length. Each extra CH₂ adds electrons and surface area, so the London (dispersion) forces between molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. The increase is largest for the first few members and gets smaller as the chain gets longer (the CH₂ is a smaller fraction of the molecule).

  • Branching lowers the boiling point: branched isomers are more compact (more spherical), so there is less surface contact and weaker London forces. Pentane (36 °C) > 2-methylbutane (28 °C) > 2,2-dimethylpropane (10 °C).
  • Functional group effect for molecules of similar mass (similar London forces): alkane < aldehyde/ketone/ether/ester (permanent dipole–dipole) < alcohol/amine (hydrogen bonding) < carboxylic acid (stronger hydrogen bonding; can form dimers).
Worked exampleArrange in order of increasing boiling point: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, CH₃COCH₃, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, CH₃COOH (all M ≈ 58–60).
1. Butane: London forces only → lowest.
2. Propanone: polar C=O → dipole–dipole as well.
3. Propan-2-ol: O–H → hydrogen bonding.
4. Ethanoic acid: two oxygen atoms; forms hydrogen-bonded dimers → highest.
Order: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ < CH₃COCH₃ < CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ < CH₃COOH.

Which isomer of C₅H₁₂ has the lowest boiling point?

  1. 2,2-dimethylpropane
  2. 2-methylbutane
  3. Pentane
  4. They are all the same

The most branched isomer is the most compact, with the least surface contact and the weakest London forces (10 °C, against 28 °C and 36 °C).

Solubility in water: short-chain alcohols, acids and amines dissolve because they form hydrogen bonds with water. As the non-polar hydrocarbon chain gets longer, solubility falls. Alkanes are insoluble in water.

S3.2.5 IUPAC nomenclature

Why bother with a system? Historical names (acetic acid, formic acid) meant nothing to chemists in other countries. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) system lets anyone draw the structure from the name.

Stem names for the longest chain: 1 C meth, 2 eth, 3 prop, 4 but, 5 pent, 6 hex. IB examines chains of up to six carbon atoms. (For completeness: 7 hept, 8 oct, 9 non, 10 dec.)

AlkaneCarbonsFormula
Methane1CH₄
Ethane2C₂H₆
Propane3C₃H₈
Butane4C₄H₁₀
Pentane5C₅H₁₂
Hexane6C₆H₁₄
Decane10C₁₀H₂₂
  1. Find the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the main functional group. This gives the stem. (It may bend round a corner in the drawing.)
  2. Add the suffix for the main functional group (-ene, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -amine…).
  3. Number the chain so that the main functional group gets the lowest possible number. If there is no functional group with a suffix, give the substituents the lowest numbers.
  4. Name the substituents as prefixes (methyl-, ethyl-, chloro-, bromo-, hydroxy-, amino-) with their locant numbers, in alphabetical order. Use di-, tri-, tetra- for repeats; these are ignored when alphabetizing.
  5. Punctuation: commas between numbers, hyphens between numbers and letters, no space before the stem: 2,3-dimethylbutane; 3-bromo-2-methylpentane.

If the carbon chain forms a ring, add the prefix cyclo: cyclohexane, cyclohexanol.

  • Aldehydes and carboxylic acids are always on carbon 1, so no number is needed: butanal, propanoic acid. The same goes for propanone and butanone (the C=O can only be on C2).
  • Older style "1-hexene" and "2-butanol" appear in some worksheets; the current IUPAC style puts the number before the suffix: hex-1-ene, butan-2-ol.
  • Esters are named from the alcohol part (alkyl) then the acid part (-oate): CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ is methyl propanoate (made from methanol + propanoic acid). The carbon chain that includes the C=O is the "-oate" part.
  • Ethers are named as alkoxyalkanes, with the smaller group as the alkoxy part: CH₃CH₂OCH₃ is methoxyethane.
  • When a suffix begins with a consonant, the "e" of the stem stays: pentane-2,4-dione (not "pentan-2,4-dione"), propane-1,2,3-triol.
Worked exampleName (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH.
1. Longest chain containing the C bearing OH: 3 carbons → prop-.
2. –OH → -ol, on C1 (numbering from the OH end).
3. A methyl group on C2.
Answer: 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
Worked exampleName CHCl₂CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
Longest chain: 5 C → pentane. Two Cl on C1 (dichloro), methyl on C3. Alphabetical order: chloro before methyl (ignore "di").
Answer: 1,1-dichloro-3-methylpentane.
Worked exampleName CH₃CH(Br)CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₃.
1. Longest chain: the CH₂CH₃ branch continues the chain, giving 5 carbons → pentane.
2. Number from the end nearer the first substituent: Br on C2, CH₃ on C3 (numbering from the other end gives 3 and 4).
3. Alphabetical order: bromo before methyl.
Answer: 2-bromo-3-methylpentane (not 2-bromo-3-ethylbutane, which uses a chain that is too short).
Worked exampleName CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)(OH)CH₃.
Longest chain with the OH: 4 C → butanol. Number to give OH the lowest number: OH on C2, methyl on C2.
Answer: 2-methylbutan-2-ol.
Worked exampleName the ester CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₃.
Acid part (contains C=O): CH₃CH₂CH₂CO– = 4 C → butanoate. Alcohol part attached to O: CH₃ → methyl.
Answer: methyl butanoate (made from methanol and butanoic acid).
Correct the mistakes: (A) "2-methyl-3-chloro-butan-4-ol" and (B) "3-methyl-2-chloro-butan-1-ol" for HOCH₂CH(Cl)CH(CH₃)CH₃

The OH must get the lowest number (C1), so Cl is on C2 and CH₃ on C3. Substituents go in alphabetical order (chloro before methyl), and there is no hyphen before the stem.

Correct name: 2-chloro-3-methylbutan-1-ol.

Correct the mistakes: "4-methyl-3-4-dichloro-3-bromo-pentane" for CH₃C(CH₃)(Cl)C(Cl)(Br)CH₂CH₃

Number from the end nearer the substituents: Cl and CH₃ on C2, Br and Cl on C3. Use commas between numbers, alphabetical order (bromo, chloro, methyl) and no hyphen before "pentane".

Correct name: 3-bromo-2,3-dichloro-2-methylpentane.

What is the correct name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂OH?

  1. 2-ethylbutan-4-ol
  2. 3-methylpentan-5-ol
  3. 3-ethylbutan-1-ol
  4. 3-methylpentan-1-ol

The longest chain containing the C–OH has 5 carbons. Number from the OH end: OH on C1, methyl on C3.

When arranging substituents alphabetically, the prefixes di-, tri- and tetra- do not count.

title: Structural isomers; primary, secondary and tertiary
html:
S3.2.6 Structural isomers

Try it with molecular models: make butane, then rearrange the atoms into a molecule with a different name. Do the same with 1-chlorobutane, and turn ethanol into a molecule with a different functional group. Record the names and displayed formulas.

DefinitionStructural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulas (the atoms are joined in a different order).

Isomerism in general means two or more compounds have the same molecular formula but a different arrangement of their atoms. Isomers have different physical and, often, chemical properties. There are two families: structural isomers (atoms bonded in a different order: chain, position and functional group isomers) and stereoisomers (atoms bonded in the same order but arranged differently in space: cis–trans/E–Z and optical; AHL).

TypeWhat changesExample
Chain (branching)The carbon skeletonC₄H₁₀: butane and 2-methylpropane
PositionPosition of the functional group on the same chainC₃H₇OH: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol; C₄H₈: but-1-ene and but-2-ene
Functional groupThe class of compoundC₃H₆O: propanal, propanone, prop-2-en-1-ol; C₂H₆O: ethanol and methoxymethane; C₃H₆O₂: propanoic acid and methyl ethanoate

Chain isomers have similar chemical properties but different boiling points; functional group isomers have different chemical and physical properties.

Worked exampleDraw and name the isomers of C₆H₁₄. There are five: hexane; 2-methylpentane; 3-methylpentane; 2,2-dimethylbutane; 2,3-dimethylbutane. (A "1-methylpentane" is just hexane, and a "4-methylpentane" is 2-methylpentane numbered the wrong way round.)
Draw all the positional isomers of C₅H₁₁Cl on an unbranched chain. Then reveal

There are three: 1-chloropentane, 2-chloropentane and 3-chloropentane. "4-chloropentane" and "5-chloropentane" are not new isomers: they are 2- and 1-chloropentane numbered from the wrong end. (Branched chains give further chain isomers, such as 1-chloro-2-methylbutane.)

How many structural isomers are there with the formula C₅H₁₂?

Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane: 3.

Propanal and propanone (both C₃H₆O) are which type of isomer?

  1. Chain isomers
  2. Position isomers
  3. Functional group isomers
  4. Optical isomers

One is an aldehyde and the other a ketone: different classes, so they are functional group isomers. (You could argue the C=O has moved position, but because the class changes, the IB calls these functional group isomers.)

Classifying alcohols, halogenoalkanes and amines

  • Alcohols and halogenoalkanes: count the carbon atoms bonded to the carbon that carries the –OH or –X. Primary (1°): one C (or none, for CH₃OH); secondary (2°): two C; tertiary (3°): three C. E.g. butan-1-ol 1°, butan-2-ol 2°, 2-methylpropan-2-ol 3°.
  • Amines are classified differently: by the number of carbon groups bonded to the nitrogen. CH₃NH₂ is 1°, (CH₃)₂NH is 2°, (CH₃)₃N is 3°.
  • This matters for reactivity (R3.2 oxidation of alcohols; R3.4 SN1/SN2 mechanisms): 1° alcohols oxidize to aldehydes then carboxylic acids, 2° to ketones, and 3° alcohols are not oxidized by acidified dichromate(VI).

Classify 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr.

  1. Primary
  2. Tertiary
  3. Secondary
  4. Quaternary

The carbon bonded to Br is attached to three other carbons, so it is a tertiary halogenoalkane.

title: Stereoisomers (AHL)
html:
S3.2.7 Stereoisomers AHL

Stereoisomers have the same molecular formula and the same structural formula (same bonding order) but a different arrangement of atoms in space. There are two kinds: cis–trans (geometric) and optical.

Cis–trans isomerism

  • Occurs because rotation about a C=C double bond is restricted (rotating would break the π bond), and in rings (e.g. 1,2-dichlorocyclopropane), where the ring prevents rotation.
  • Condition: each carbon of the C=C must carry two different groups. But-2-ene has cis and trans forms; but-1-ene (one carbon carries H and H) and methylpropene do not.
  • Cis: the two identical (or matching) groups are on the same side; trans: on opposite sides. Cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene.
  • When all four groups are different, the E/Z system is used. On each carbon, rank the two groups by atomic number of the attached atom (higher Z = higher priority). Z (zusammen, "together"): the two higher-priority groups are on the same side. E (entgegen, "opposite"): on opposite sides.
  • Cis and trans isomers have different physical properties. The cis isomer is often polar (dipoles do not cancel) and may have a higher boiling point; the trans isomer packs better in a solid and often has a higher melting point. Cis-but-2-enedioic acid can lose water on heating to form a cyclic anhydride because its two COOH groups are close together; the trans isomer cannot.

Example: for 1,2-dichloroethene, the cis (Z) isomer melts at −80 °C and boils at 60 °C, while the trans (E) isomer melts at −50 °C and boils at 48 °C. E and Z isomers can also react differently with biological molecules.

Common mistake"Z" and "cis" usually coincide but not always: Z/E depends on priorities, cis/trans on identical groups. If a deuterium atom is present, it has the same atomic number as H, so the tie is broken by mass: D outranks H.
Worked exampleOne carbon of a C=C carries Br and Cl; the other carries CH₂CH₃ and H. Br and CH₂CH₃ are on the same side. Name it.
1. Chain: C=C plus the ethyl → 4 carbons, double bond at C1 → but-1-ene, with Br and Cl on C1: 1-bromo-1-chlorobut-1-ene.
2. Priorities on C1: Br (Z = 35) > Cl (17). On C2: CH₂CH₃ (C, Z = 6) > H (1).
3. Br and CH₂CH₃ are on the same side → Z.
Answer: (Z)-1-bromo-1-chlorobut-1-ene.
Spotting E/Z isomers: which of these can exist as E and Z forms? methylpropene, 1-chloropropene, 2-methylpent-2-ene, 2-ethylpent-1-ene, 3-methylpent-2-ene, but-1-ene, 3,4-dimethylhex-3-ene, 2-bromo-3-chlorobut-2-ene

Yes: 1-chloropropene, 3-methylpent-2-ene, 3,4-dimethylhex-3-ene, 2-bromo-3-chlorobut-2-ene.

No: methylpropene (C1 has two H and C2 has two CH₃), 2-methylpent-2-ene (C2 carries two CH₃), 2-ethylpent-1-ene (C1 carries two H) and but-1-ene (C1 carries two H). One carbon with two identical groups is enough to rule out E/Z isomerism.

Which compound shows cis–trans isomerism?

  1. CH₂=CHCl
  2. (CH₃)₂C=CH₂
  3. CH₃CH=CHCH₃
  4. CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃

In but-2-ene each C of the C=C carries H and CH₃ (two different groups). In the others, at least one carbon of the C=C carries two identical groups.

Optical isomerism

  • A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is a chiral centre (stereocentre, asymmetric carbon), often marked with *.
  • A molecule with one chiral centre exists as two enantiomers: non-superimposable mirror images of each other. Draw them in 3-D with wedges and dashes as mirror images.
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties (m.p., b.p., density) and identical chemical properties with non-chiral reagents. They differ in how they rotate the plane of plane-polarized light: equal angles, opposite directions. This is measured with a polarimeter. They may also react differently with other chiral molecules (e.g. enzymes, receptors), which is why one enantiomer of a drug may be active and the other inactive or harmful.
  • A racemic mixture (racemate) contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers. It does not rotate plane-polarized light because the rotations cancel.
  • A molecule with n chiral centres can have up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers.
Worked exampleWhich are chiral? (from your class task)
Butan-2-ol: C2 carries H, OH, CH₃, C₂H₅ → four different groups → chiral.
Propan-2-ol: C2 carries two CH₃ groups → not chiral.
2-chlorobutane, 3-methylhexane, 2-methylbutanoic acid, 1-chloro-3-methylpentane → chiral. 1-chlorobutane and butanone → not chiral.

Which molecule is chiral?

  1. Propan-2-ol
  2. Pentan-3-ol
  3. 1-chlorobutane
  4. 2-chlorobutane

In 2-chlorobutane C2 carries H, Cl, CH₃ and C₂H₅: four different groups. Propan-2-ol has two CH₃ on C2; pentan-3-ol has two C₂H₅ on C3; 1-chlorobutane has no carbon with four different groups.

Worked exampleHow many optical isomers does isoleucine, CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH(NH₂)COOH, have?
C3 carries H, CH₃, C₂H₅ and CH(NH₂)COOH → chiral. C2 carries H, NH₂, COOH and the rest of the chain → chiral.
Two chiral centres → 2² = 4 stereoisomers.

A molecule has three chiral centres (and no other stereo-elements). What is the maximum number of stereoisomers?

2ⁿ = 2³ = 8.
Common mistakeCheck each carbon properly: a CH₂ or CH₃ carbon can never be chiral (it has two or three identical H atoms). Also, "different groups" means the whole group: in pentan-3-ol, C3 carries two identical ethyl groups, so it is not chiral.

title: Mass spectrometry of organic compounds (AHL)
html:
S3.2.8 Mass spectrometry of organic compounds AHL

Do now: what is mass spectrometry, what do we use it for, and what are the steps?

Recap from SL: how a mass spectrometer works

A mass spectrometer measures the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of ions. It is used to find relative atomic masses and isotope abundances, and the molecular mass and structure of unknown compounds. Uses today include monitoring patients' breath during surgery, detecting banned substances in athletes, analysing molecules in space and detecting toxic chemicals in marine life.

Use the magnesium spectrum (79% ²⁴Mg, 10% ²⁵Mg, 11% ²⁶Mg) to calculate Ar(Mg) to 2 decimal places.

Ar = (79 × 24 + 10 × 25 + 11 × 26)/100 = (1896 + 250 + 286)/100 = 24.32. (The data-booklet value is 24.31; these rounded abundances give 24.32.)

Calculate Ar(Zr) from the spectrum.

(51.5 × 90 + 11.2 × 91 + 17.1 × 92 + 17.4 × 94 + 2.8 × 96)/100 = 9131.8/100 = 91.32 (data booklet 91.22).

Molecules: the molecular ion

In a mass spectrometer, gaseous molecules are bombarded with high-energy electrons, which knock out one electron to form the molecular ion, M⁺:

M(g) + e⁻ → M⁺(g) + 2e⁻    e.g. C₂H₅OH(g) + e⁻ → C₂H₅OH⁺(g) + 2e⁻

The mass of the lost electron is negligible, so the m/z of the molecular ion equals the relative molecular mass.

  • The molecular ion peak (usually the peak with the highest m/z) gives the relative molecular mass Mr. (A tiny M+1 peak from ¹³C can appear just beyond it.)
  • Excess energy makes the molecular ion vibrate and break apart (fragmentation). Only the positive fragment is detected; the neutral radical is not. For example, CH₃CH₂OH⁺ → CH₂OH⁺ (m/z 31) + CH₃•.
  • The tallest peak is the base peak (most abundant, most stable ion), set to 100%.
  • Isomers have the same M⁺ but different fragmentation patterns, so the pattern acts as a fingerprint that can be matched against a database.
Methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, is a structural isomer of ethanol. Predict how its mass spectrum would differ

Both have M⁺ at 46. Methoxymethane would show a peak at 31 for CH₃O⁺ and a peak at 15 for CH₃⁺. It cannot give C₂H₅⁺ (29) or OH⁺ (17), because it has no C–C bond and no O–H bond, so those ethanol peaks would be missing.

m/z of fragment ionLikely ion
15CH₃⁺
29C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺
31CH₂OH⁺ / CH₃O⁺
43C₃H₇⁺ or CH₃CO⁺
45COOH⁺
57C₄H₉⁺ or C₂H₅CO⁺
77C₆H₅⁺
Peak atNeutral group lost from M⁺
M − 15CH₃
M − 17OH
M − 18H₂O
M − 28CO or C₂H₄
M − 29C₂H₅ or CHO
M − 31CH₃O
M − 45COOH

(Common fragments and losses are listed in the data booklet; use it.)

Worked exampleA ketone, C₃H₆O, has peaks at m/z 58, 43 and 15. Interpret them.
m/z 58 = M⁺, CH₃COCH₃⁺ (Mr = 58).
m/z 43 = CH₃CO⁺ (loss of CH₃, M − 15). This is the base peak.
m/z 15 = CH₃⁺.
Compound: propanone. (Propanal, its isomer, would show a strong m/z 29 peak from CHO⁺/C₂H₅⁺ instead.)
What could the alkane with M⁺ = 86 be?

Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: 14n + 2 = 86 gives n = 6, so it is C₆H₁₄, an isomer of hexane. The spaced-out fragments 29, 43, 57, 71 (each 14 apart, one CH₂) fit an unbranched chain: hexane.

A mass spectrum has peaks at m/z 15, 29, 43, 45 and 60 (M⁺). Which compound fits?

  1. Propan-1-ol
  2. Ethanoic acid
  3. Methyl methanoate
  4. Propanal

M = 60 fits C₂H₄O₂ or C₃H₈O. The peak at 45 is COOH⁺ and 15 is CH₃⁺: CH₃COOH. Losing OH gives CH₃CO⁺ at 43. Propanal has M = 58.

Suggest the ions responsible for peaks A, B and C in the pent-1-ene spectrum

A (m/z 70): the molecular ion, C₅H₁₀⁺.
B (m/z 55): C₄H₇⁺, from loss of CH₃ (70 − 15).
C (m/z 27–29): a small fragment such as C₂H₃⁺ (27) or C₂H₅⁺ (29).

Exam tipFragments must be written with a positive charge (C₂H₅⁺, not C₂H₅). When asked for an equation, show the cation and a neutral species: CH₃COCH₃⁺ → CH₃CO⁺ + CH₃.
Summary questions: (1) ionization equations for nonane and butan-1-ol; (2) why is there sometimes a small peak just beyond M⁺? (3) identify m/z 29 and 31 from butan-1-ol; (4) hexan-2-one gives a large peak at m/z 43: suggest two structures and equations

(1) C₉H₂₀(g) + e⁻ → C₉H₂₀⁺(g) + 2e⁻ (m/z 128); C₄H₉OH(g) + e⁻ → C₄H₉OH⁺(g) + 2e⁻ (m/z 74).

(2) It is the M+1 peak: about 1.1% of carbon atoms are ¹³C, so a few molecular ions are one unit heavier. (It is not "noise" from vibration.)

(3) 29 = C₂H₅⁺; 31 = CH₂OH⁺.

(4) CH₃CO⁺ or CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺. C₆H₁₂O⁺ → CH₃CO⁺ + C₄H₉; C₆H₁₂O⁺ → CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ + C₃H₅O.

title: Infrared spectroscopy (AHL)
html:
S3.2.9 Infrared (IR) spectroscopy AHL

Do now: write down the order of the waves in the electromagnetic spectrum, from lowest energy to highest. Mnemonic: Reindeer Meat Is a Very Unusual Xmas Gift (radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma).

Electromagnetic waves consist of electric and magnetic fields that are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, vibrating at the same frequency. Atoms, molecules and ions absorb (or emit) radiation of specific frequencies, which can be used to identify them.

Different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum cause different changes in molecules: UV/visible light promotes electrons (used for colour, S3.1), IR makes bonds vibrate, radio waves change nuclear spin (NMR).

Which radiation is used in NMR spectroscopy?

  1. Infrared
  2. Ultraviolet
  3. Microwaves
  4. Radio waves

The energy needed to flip a nuclear spin in a magnetic field is very small, corresponding to radio frequencies. IR causes bond vibrations; UV promotes electrons; microwaves cause rotation.

Bond vibrations

  • Covalent bonds vibrate (stretch and bend) at natural frequencies in the infrared region. A bond absorbs IR radiation of the same frequency, so the radiation that passes through is reduced at that frequency.
  • The frequency depends on bond strength (stronger = higher wavenumber) and the masses of the atoms (lighter atoms = higher wavenumber, which is why bonds to H appear above 2500 cm⁻¹), and on the type of vibration.
  • A vibration only absorbs IR if it causes a change in dipole moment (the molecule is "IR active"). That is why H₂O, CO₂ and CH₄ absorb IR (greenhouse gases), while N₂ and O₂ do not. In CO₂ the symmetric stretch is IR inactive (the dipoles still cancel), but the asymmetric stretch and bending are active.
  • Spectra plot % transmittance against wavenumber (cm⁻¹, = 1/wavelength), so absorptions appear as downward dips.
BondTypical compoundWavenumber / cm⁻¹Appearance
O–HAlcohols3200–3600Strong, broad (hydrogen bonding)
N–HAmines, amides3300–3500Medium, sharper
C–HMost organic compounds2850–3090Medium–strong
O–HCarboxylic acids2500–3000Very broad, overlaps C–H
C≡C / C≡NAlkynes / nitriles2100–2260Medium, sharp
C=OAldehydes, ketones, acids, esters, amides1700–1750Strong, sharp
C=CAlkenes1620–1680Medium–weak
C–OAlcohols, ethers, esters1050–1410Strong
  • Above 1500 cm⁻¹ is the functional group region. Below 1500 cm⁻¹ is the fingerprint region: too many overlapping peaks to assign, but the pattern is unique to the compound and can be matched to a database.
  • Distinguishing the "O" compounds: alcohol = broad O–H at 3200–3600, no C=O; aldehyde/ketone = sharp C=O at ~1720, no O–H; carboxylic acid = very broad O–H at 2500–3000 and C=O; ester = C=O and C–O, no O–H.
  • Uses: breathalysers (absorption by bonds in ethanol), forensic paint analysis, monitoring the degree of unsaturation in polymers, quality control in perfume manufacture, drug analysis, and monitoring the oxidation of an alcohol to a carboxylic acid.

Breathalysers: a roadside device gives an indication of breath alcohol; the evidential instrument at the police station uses an IR spectrometer and measures the size of an absorption by ethanol. In practice these instruments usually measure a C–H (about 2950 cm⁻¹) or C–O absorption, because the water vapour in breath also absorbs strongly in the O–H region.

Common mistakeIR tells you which bonds (and therefore functional groups) are present. It does not give the molar mass (MS), the number of H environments (NMR) or the 3-D shape (X-ray crystallography). If a markscheme asks for the functional group from a 1715 cm⁻¹ peak, answer "C=O / carbonyl", not "ketone": an aldehyde, acid or ester would also fit.

An organic compound absorbs at 1700 cm⁻¹ and has no absorption above 3000 cm⁻¹. Which functional group must be present?

  1. C=O (carbonyl)
  2. O–H (alcohol)
  3. O–H (carboxylic acid)
  4. C=C

1700 cm⁻¹ is C=O. No broad band above 3000 rules out an alcohol, and the absence of a very broad 2500–3300 band rules out a carboxylic acid. It could be an aldehyde, ketone or ester.

IR problems

Choose from: hex-2-ene, pentane, methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpentan-3-one, butanal, butanoic acid, propyl ethanoate, nitrobenzene.

Which compound gives spectrum 3?

  1. Butanoic acid
  2. Butanal
  3. Methylpropan-1-ol
  4. Propyl ethanoate

A strong, broad band at about 3350 cm⁻¹ is an alcohol O–H, and there is no C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹. The strong peak near 1040 cm⁻¹ is C–O.

Which compound gives spectrum 7?

  1. Butanoic acid
  2. Methylpropan-1-ol
  3. Hex-2-ene
  4. Nitrobenzene

A very broad O–H spreading over 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ together with a strong C=O near 1710 cm⁻¹ is the signature of a carboxylic acid.

Which compound gives spectrum 1?

  1. Butanal
  2. Pentane
  3. Butanoic acid
  4. Propyl ethanoate

C=O at about 1740 cm⁻¹ plus a strong C–O at about 1240 cm⁻¹, with no O–H at all: an ester.

Reveal the labelled answers for spectra 1, 3, 6 and 7
More practice: which of propanoic acid, butanone, 2-methylbut-2-ene, 1-hydroxypropan-2-one and butan-2-ol has both a broad O–H and a C=O? Which has only C=O?

Propanoic acid and 1-hydroxypropan-2-one both show O–H and C=O (the acid's O–H is much broader and lower, 2500–3300 cm⁻¹; the hydroxyketone's O–H is an alcohol band near 3400 cm⁻¹). Butanone shows only C=O. Butan-2-ol shows only O–H. 2-methylbut-2-ene shows neither (C–H and a weak C=C).

Review questions: (1) explain how covalent bonds are affected by IR radiation; (2) give approximate key wavenumbers for pentan-2-ol, 2-hydroxypentanal and butanoic acid

(1) Bonds absorb IR radiation of their natural frequency, which increases the amplitude of their stretching or bending vibrations (only if the dipole moment changes).

(2) Pentan-2-ol: O–H 3200–3600 (and C–O 1050–1410). 2-hydroxypentanal: O–H 3200–3600 and C=O 1700–1750. Butanoic acid: O–H 2500–3000 (very broad) and C=O 1700–1750.

title: ¹H NMR spectroscopy (AHL)
html:
S3.2.10 ¹H NMR spectroscopy AHL

Do now: discuss with the person next to you what you already know about NMR.

NMR is an analytical technique used to work out the structure of molecules. Paired with IR and mass spectrometry, it can be used to predict the structures of organic molecules with confidence. ¹³C NMR also exists, but in IB Chemistry we only interpret proton (¹H) NMR.

  • ¹H nuclei (protons) have nuclear spin and behave like tiny magnets. In a strong magnetic field they can align with or against it; absorbing radio-frequency radiation flips them to the higher-energy state.
  • Only nuclei with an odd number of nucleons (an odd mass number), such as ¹H and ¹³C, have this spin; nuclei with even numbers of both protons and neutrons, such as ¹²C and ¹⁶O, have zero spin and give no signal.
  • The exact frequency depends on the chemical environment of each H: nearby electronegative atoms or groups pull electron density away (deshielding), so the signal appears further left (higher δ).
  • Chemical shift, δ, is measured in ppm relative to the reference TMS, tetramethylsilane Si(CH₃)₄, set at δ = 0.

Think of it like tuning a radio: the frequency is changed gradually, and each type of proton "comes into tune" at its own frequency. The amount of shielding, and so the energy absorbed, is called the chemical shift.

Key pointWhy TMS? All 12 H atoms are in the same environment, so it gives one strong, sharp signal; the signal is upfield of (well away from) almost all organic signals; it is inert, non-toxic and volatile, so it is easily removed from the sample. Solvents without ¹H, such as CDCl₃ or CCl₄, are used so the solvent gives no signal.

Proton environments

Think about your own environment in a classroom: it is the people around you, and it changes depending on whether your best friend sits next to you or across the room. A proton's environment is the atoms it is bonded to and the order they are bonded in. Protons in different environments have different chemical shifts, and each environment produces one signal.

How many proton environments are there in propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃?

The two CH₃ groups are equivalent by symmetry, and the CH₂ is different: 2 environments (6 : 2 = 3 : 1).
Answers: butane, propan-1-ol, benzene, and the methyl-substituted phenol shown

Butane: 2 (CH₃ ×2, CH₂ ×2). Propan-1-ol: 4 (CH₃, CH₂, CH₂O, OH). Benzene: 1 (all six H equivalent). The ring with OH and CH₃ opposite each other (4-methylphenol): 4 (OH, CH₃, and two pairs of ring H).

A (low-resolution) ¹H NMR spectrum tells you three things:

  1. Number of signals = number of different H environments. H atoms on the same carbon are equivalent, and symmetry makes groups equivalent (both CH₃ groups in propanone are the same environment).
  2. Chemical shift of each signal (look it up in the data booklet) = the type of environment.
  3. Relative peak area (from the integration trace: measure the step heights) = the ratio of H atoms in each environment.
Type of protonδ / ppm (approx.)
R–CH₃, R–CH₂–R (alkyl)0.9–1.5
CH₃–CO– / –CH₂–CO– (next to C=O)2.0–2.7
C₆H₅–CH₂– (next to benzene ring)2.5–3.5
R–O–CH₂– (ether, alcohol)3.3–3.7
CH₂–Hal3.5–4.4
R–COO–CH₂– (on the O side of an ester)3.7–4.8
R–O–H (alcohol)1.0–6.0 (variable)
–CH=CH₂ (alkene)4.5–6.0
C₆H₅–H (benzene ring)6.9–9.0
R–CHO (aldehyde)9.4–10.0
R–COOH (carboxylic acid)9.0–13.0
Worked examplePredict the low-resolution spectrum of ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH.
Environments: CH₃ (3 H), CH₂ (2 H), OH (1 H) → 3 signals, area ratio 3 : 2 : 1.
Shifts: CH₃ ≈ 1.2 ppm (alkyl); CH₂ ≈ 3.6 ppm (next to O); OH variable (~2–5 ppm).

Relative intensities: the areas give the simplest whole-number ratio of H atoms in each environment, not the actual numbers. For example 1.2 : 1.2 : 1.8 = 2 : 2 : 3; 2.1 : 2.8 = 3 : 4; 1.5 : 0.5 : 2.0 = 3 : 1 : 4; 0.3 : 0.15 : 0.3 : 0.6 = 2 : 1 : 2 : 4.

Integration step heights are 0.8 cm, 1.2 cm and 2.0 cm. What is the simplest ratio of H atoms?

  1. 4 : 6 : 8
  2. 2 : 3 : 5
  3. 1 : 1 : 2
  4. 8 : 12 : 2

Divide by the smallest (0.8 → 1 : 1.5 : 2.5) and double to get whole numbers: 2 : 3 : 5.

Worked exampleFind the area ratio for 2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃.
The two CH₃ groups on C2 are equivalent (6 H); the CH (1 H); the CH₂ (2 H); the end CH₃ (3 H). → 4 signals, 6 : 1 : 2 : 3.
And pentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃: symmetrical → 2 × CH₃ (6 H), 2 × CH₂ (4 H), CH (1 H), OH (1 H) → 6 : 4 : 1 : 1.
Exam tipTo tell isomers apart, NMR is usually the best technique. Propan-1-ol has 4 signals (3:2:2:1) but propan-2-ol only 3 (6:1:1), even though their mass spectra share M⁺ = 60 and their IR spectra look very similar.

S3.2.11 High-resolution ¹H NMR: splitting patterns AHL

In a high-resolution spectrum you see small clusters of lines rather than single signals. In a high-resolution spectrum, a signal is split by the H atoms on neighbouring (adjacent) carbon atoms. This is spin–spin coupling, and the splitting pattern tells you how many protons are in the environment next door.

Key pointThe n + 1 rule: a signal from H atoms with n equivalent H atoms on adjacent carbons is split into (n + 1) peaks. Relative peak heights follow Pascal's triangle.
Neighbouring H (n)Peaks (n + 1)NameHeight ratio
01singlet1
12doublet1 : 1
23triplet1 : 2 : 1
34quartet1 : 3 : 3 : 1
45quintet1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1
  • Equivalent H atoms do not split each other. The O–H proton of an alcohol or acid usually appears as a singlet (it exchanges rapidly) and does not split neighbours.
  • Coupled signals share the same gap between peaks (the coupling constant), which shows which groups are next to each other.
  • Classic pattern: a triplet (3 H) + quartet (2 H) means an ethyl group, CH₃CH₂–. A 6 H doublet + 1 H multiplet (septet) means an isopropyl group, (CH₃)₂CH–.

Example: butanone, CH₃CH₂COCH₃, gives a triplet at about 1.0 ppm (the CH₃ of the ethyl group, next to a CH₂: 2 + 1 = 3), a singlet at about 2.1 ppm (the CH₃ next to C=O, which has no H neighbours) and a quartet at about 2.4 ppm (the CH₂, next to a CH₃: 3 + 1 = 4).

Worked examplePredict the high-resolution spectrum of ethanal, CH₃CHO.
CH₃ (2.2 ppm, 3 H): neighbouring CHO has 1 H → doublet.
CHO (9.8 ppm, 1 H): neighbouring CH₃ has 3 H → quartet.

In 1-chloropropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl, what is the splitting of the CH₃ signal?

  1. Singlet
  2. Doublet
  3. Triplet
  4. Quartet

The CH₃ is next to a CH₂ (2 H), so n + 1 = 3: a triplet.

Predict the number of signals, ratio and splitting for: methylpropene, propanone, 2-chloropropane, ethyl propanoate, 1,2-dibromopropane, but-2-ene
CompoundSignalsRatioSplitting
Methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂23 : 1 (6 : 2)s, s
Propanone, CH₃COCH₃1—s (2.1–2.6 ppm)
2-chloropropane, (CH₃)₂CHCl26 : 1d, m (septet)
Ethyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃43 : 2 : 2 : 3t, q, q, t
1,2-dibromopropane, CH₂BrCHBrCH₃32 : 1 : 3d, m, d
But-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃23 : 1d, q

Methylamine, CH₃NH₂, gives two signals (3 : 2); at this level both appear as singlets, because N–H protons exchange and usually do not couple.

Markscheme for compound J

(i) CDCl₃ (or CD₂Cl₂, C₆D₆, CCl₄); not D₂O.
(ii) 4 peaks: the two CH₃ groups (6 H), the ClCH₂ on the quaternary carbon (2 H, singlet), the CH₂ labelled a and the CH₂Cl at the end.
(iii) Triplet: protons a are next to one CH₂ (2 H); the quaternary carbon has no H.
(iv) 1,4-dichloro-2,2-dimethylbutane.

title: Index of hydrogen deficiency and combining techniques (AHL)
html:
S3.2.12 Index of hydrogen deficiency and combining techniques AHL

Saturated compounds hold the maximum number of H atoms; every ring or π bond means two fewer H atoms. The IHD lets you read this from the molecular formula before you look at any spectrum.

DefinitionThe index of hydrogen deficiency (IHD), or degree of unsaturation, is the number of H₂ molecules that would have to be added to make the molecule saturated and acyclic. Each ring or double bond counts 1; each triple bond counts 2; a benzene ring counts 4 (one ring + three C=C).
IHD = (2C + 2 + N − H − X) / 2

C = number of carbons, H = hydrogens, N = nitrogens, X = halogens. Oxygen and sulfur atoms are ignored.

Equivalent rules: treat each halogen atom as a hydrogen; for each nitrogen atom, add one C and one H to the formula; ignore O and S; then use IHD = (2C + 2 − H)/2.

Worked example(a) 3-methylcyclohexene, C₇H₁₂: IHD = (14 + 2 − 12)/2 = 2 (one ring + one C=C).
(b) C₈H₈O₂ (an ester with a phenyl group): IHD = (16 + 2 − 8)/2 = 5 (benzene ring = 4, C=O = 1).
(c) C₂H₃Cl: IHD = (4 + 2 − 3 − 1)/2 = 1 (chloroethene, one C=C).

Calculate the IHD of benzene, C₆H₆.

(2 × 6 + 2 − 6)/2 = 8/2 = 4: one ring and three C=C.

Calculate the IHD of C₄H₅N.

(2 × 4 + 2 + 1 − 5)/2 = 6/2 = 3. Remember to add 1 for each N. (Pyrrole, C₄H₅N, has one ring and two C=C.)

A compound C₅H₈ does not decolorize bromine water. What is its most likely structure type?

  1. A diene
  2. Two rings (or a ring system with no C=C)
  3. An alkyne
  4. A single ring with a C=C

IHD = (10 + 2 − 8)/2 = 2. With no C=C or C≡C (no reaction with bromine), both units of unsaturation must be rings, e.g. bicyclo[2.1.0]pentane or spiropentane.

Combining techniques to identify an unknown (a typical Paper 2 question):

  1. Use % composition by mass to get the empirical formula (S1.4).
  2. Use the M⁺ peak in the mass spectrum to get Mr and the molecular formula.
  3. Calculate the IHD to see how many rings/π bonds there are.
  4. Use IR to find the functional groups (O–H? C=O? both?).
  5. Use ¹H NMR (number of signals, shifts, ratio, splitting) to assemble the carbon skeleton.
  6. Check the proposed structure against every piece of data, including MS fragments.
Worked exampleAn unknown contains 62.02% C and 10.43% H by mass; the rest is O.
1. Moles in 100 g: C 62.02/12.01 = 5.164; H 10.43/1.01 = 10.33; O 27.55/16.00 = 1.722. Divide by 1.722 → 3 : 6 : 1 → C₃H₆O.
2. MS: M⁺ at m/z 58 → molecular formula C₃H₆O. Base peak at 43 (CH₃CO⁺), peak at 15 (CH₃⁺).
3. IHD = (6 + 2 − 6)/2 = 1 → one C=O or C=C or ring.
4. IR: strong 1715 cm⁻¹ (C=O), no broad 3200–3600 (no O–H).
5. ¹H NMR: one singlet (6 H) at about 2.2 ppm → two equivalent CH₃ groups next to C=O.
6. Not oxidized by acidified dichromate(VI) → a ketone, not an aldehyde.
Answer: propanone, CH₃COCH₃.
Worked exampleC₈H₈O₂ contains a phenyl group. IR: 1724 cm⁻¹ (C=O), 1280 and 1110 cm⁻¹ (C–O), no O–H. ¹H NMR: 7.4–8.1 ppm (5 H, multiplet) and 3.9 ppm (3 H, singlet).
5 H at 7.4–8.1 → C₆H₅–. 3 H singlet at 3.9 ppm → CH₃ attached to the ester O (3.7–4.8 range). C=O + C–O, no O–H → ester.
Answer: methyl benzoate, C₆H₅COOCH₃. (Its isomer phenyl ethanoate, CH₃COOC₆H₅, would have its CH₃ singlet at about 2.0–2.5 ppm, next to the C=O.)
Exam question: the ¹H NMR spectrum of C₄H₈O₂ shows signals with areas 3 : 2 : 3 as a triplet, quartet and singlet; the singlet is at about 3.7 ppm. Its IR spectrum shows 1740 cm⁻¹ and no O–H. Identify it

IHD = (8 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1: the C=O. C=O with no O–H → an ester. A triplet (3 H) + quartet (2 H) = an ethyl group next to C=O (quartet at about 2.3 ppm); a 3 H singlet at 3.7 ppm = CH₃ on the ester oxygen. Answer: methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃. (Ethyl ethanoate would have its quartet at about 4.1 ppm, on the O side, and its singlet at about 2.0 ppm.)

Exam question: (a) C₆H₄N₂O₄ compounds F and G are both dinitrobenzenes; F has two peaks and G three in their ¹³C NMR spectra. (b) C₆H₁₂ compounds H and J each have one ¹H NMR peak; H reacts with bromine water but J does not. Suggest structures

(a) F: 1,4-dinitrobenzene (high symmetry: two carbon environments). G: 1,2-dinitrobenzene (three carbon environments).

(b) H: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂ (all 12 H equivalent; the C=C reacts with bromine). J: cyclohexane (all 12 H equivalent; saturated, so no reaction).

Exam question: K and L are cyclic C₆H₁₀O compounds with four peaks in their ¹³C NMR spectra; K is a ketone and L an aldehyde. M and N are C₆H₁₅N amines: M is tertiary with two ¹H peaks; N is secondary with three ¹H peaks. Suggest structures

K: cyclohexanone (C=O, C2/C6, C3/C5, C4: four carbon environments), or 3,3-dimethylcyclobutanone, or 2,4-dimethylcyclobutanone. L: cyclopentanecarbaldehyde (CHO, C1, C2/C5, C3/C4), or 2,3-dimethylcyclopropanecarbaldehyde.

M: triethylamine, (CH₃CH₂)₃N (two ¹H environments: CH₃ and CH₂), or (CH₃)₂NC(CH₃)₃. N: di(propan-2-yl)amine, ((CH₃)₂CH)₂NH (three environments: CH₃, CH, NH).

X-ray crystallography is used to find the precise 3-D arrangement of atoms in a crystal: X-rays are diffracted by the electron density, and the diffraction pattern gives bond lengths and bond angles. It can locate every atom except, usually, hydrogen (too little electron density), and it is the only one of these techniques that gives the full 3-D shape, including the configuration of chiral centres.

TechniqueMain informationRadiation / process
Mass spectrometryMr (M⁺) and fragmentsElectron bombardment; breaks bonds
IRBonds / functional groups presentInfrared; bond vibrations
¹H NMRH environments, ratio, neighboursRadio waves; nuclear spin flip
X-ray crystallographyBond lengths, angles, 3-D structureX-ray diffraction by electron density

Which technique breaks covalent bonds in the sample?

  1. Mass spectrometry
  2. IR spectroscopy
  3. ¹H NMR spectroscopy
  4. X-ray crystallography

Electron bombardment ionizes and fragments the molecule. IR and NMR only excite vibrations or nuclear spins, and X-ray crystallography diffracts off the crystal.

Exam tipMass spectrometry is the technique that breaks covalent bonds in the sample. IR and NMR leave the molecule intact.
